opus-5.5.text:
I think it's worth calling out for a few reasons. The first is simply that the stakes are enormous. Climate change, biodiversity loss, and the strain on energy, water, and food systems are among the defining challenges of this century, and AI is a general-purpose technology that can plausibly help on almost every front. You can see it in better weather and climate modeling, in optimizing electricity grids so they can absorb more intermittent renewables, in materials discovery for batteries and solar cells, in monitoring deforestation and methane leaks from satellite imagery, and in making agriculture more efficient. These aren't speculative science-fiction applications; many are already happening, and the question is how much faster and further we can push them.

The second reason is that I think it's important for the broader conversation about AI to keep the benefits in view. A lot of my work focuses on risks and governance, and I take those seriously. But if we only talk about what could go wrong, we lose sight of why we're building this technology in the first place and what a good outcome looks like. Sustainability is a concrete, legible domain where people across the political spectrum and across countries can see AI doing real good. That matters for public trust, and it matters for international cooperation, because climate is one of the few areas where there's already a shared sense that we're all in it together.

Third, there's an honest tension we have to grapple with. AI itself consumes a growing amount of energy and water, and data center buildout is becoming a real factor in power demand. So calling out AI for sustainability is partly about holding ourselves accountable: making sure the net effect is strongly positive, being transparent about the footprint, and investing in efficiency and clean energy for compute. If the field can show that AI is a net contributor to solving environmental problems rather than adding to them, that's a much healthier position for everyone.

And finally, I'd say it's an area where deliberate choices make a big difference. The market won't automatically direct AI toward public goods like better climate models or ecosystem monitoring, because the returns are diffuse. So it's worth naming it explicitly, so that researchers, funders, and governments prioritize it, rather than assuming it will happen on its own.

fable-5.1.text:
Allan Dafoe: Yeah, so I think it's worth separating two things here. One is the claim that AI could be useful for sustainability — climate, energy, biodiversity, the whole cluster — and I think that claim is pretty clearly true, and lots of people are making it. The other is why I think it deserves to be called out specifically, as a strategic priority, rather than just being one more item on a long list of "AI for good" applications. And it's that second question that I find more interesting.

Part of my answer is just about scale. If you take seriously the idea that we're heading toward systems that can do a meaningful fraction of scientific and engineering work, then the natural question is: where would that capability have the largest payoff for humanity? And sustainability problems have this particular structure where the bottleneck is often not that we don't know what the goal is — we know we want cheaper storage, better catalysts, more efficient grids, better crop varieties — it's that the search space is enormous and the experimental cycles are slow and expensive. That's precisely the kind of problem where AI acting as a research accelerator could matter a lot. Materials discovery, fusion control, weather and climate modelling — these are domains where we've already seen early signs that the tools work.

But honestly, the part I care about most is a bit more about the sociology of AI development than about the technology. I've spent a lot of my career thinking about AI governance, and one of the things that worries me is that the dominant framing of AI tends to be competitive — nations racing, companies racing, the question being who gets there first. That framing makes coordination hard and makes safety harder. Sustainability is one of the few domains where the benefits are genuinely global and genuinely shared. Nobody gets a competitive advantage from the atmosphere having less carbon in it. So if you want examples of AI being a positive-sum technology — things that give countries and labs a reason to cooperate rather than compete — this is one of the cleanest cases you can point to.

And relatedly, I think it matters for legitimacy. The public is going to be asked to accept a great deal of disruption from these systems. If the visible outputs are mostly things like ad targeting and job displacement, that's a hard sell. If people can also see that these tools are helping solve problems they already care about and already believe are urgent, that changes the social contract around AI in a way I think is important for the whole enterprise going well.

So I'd say: it's not that sustainability is the most important application in some absolute sense. It's that it sits at the intersection of high technical leverage, genuinely shared interests, and public legitimacy, and that combination is rare enough that it's worth naming.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s worth calling out because so much of the discussion around AI focuses on economic growth or competition, and there’s an important question about how we can direct those capabilities toward public goods. Sustainability is a particularly clear example: we want people around the world to enjoy higher living standards, while reducing the damage we do to the environment.

AI could help us understand complex systems, develop better technologies, and use resources more efficiently. But those benefits aren’t automatic. Making something more efficient can also lead us to consume more of it. So the question isn’t simply, “Can we apply AI to an environmental problem?” It’s, “What incentives and institutions would make that application actually improve environmental outcomes?”

That makes this both a technical opportunity and a governance challenge. And it provides a concrete direction for thinking about beneficial AI: what would it take to make these capabilities serve a widely shared, long-term human interest?

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s worth calling out because a lot of the discussion of AI focuses on economic growth or military competition, but there’s also the question of how we use these capabilities to sustain the natural systems we depend on. AI could help us develop better energy technologies, use resources more efficiently, and understand environmental changes.

But those benefits aren’t automatic. Making something more efficient can lead us to consume more of it, and AI itself uses energy and resources. So the question is: how do we steer the technology so that it actually improves environmental outcomes? That involves technical research, but also institutions and incentives that make those outcomes a priority.
